Stage 3 · Reading

Three rooms people had built for thinking in

What designers actually change about their own workspaces — and why it is usually the opposite of what the brochures promise.

🎨🪑
1 · Before you read. A company knocks down the internal walls of its office. What happens to the amount of talking?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against paragraph 1.

Three rooms people had built for thinking in

Written for this course. Research finding from Bernstein & Turban, ‘The impact of the “open” workspace on human collaboration’, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 373:20170239 (2018). The three profiles are composites.

1The standard argument for the open office is that removing walls makes people talk to each other. In 2018 two researchers tested it properly, tracking employees at two corporate headquarters with wearable sensors and message logs before and after the walls came down. Face-to-face interaction fell by roughly seventy per cent in both cases, and email and instant messaging rose to replace it. People who could be seen at all times withdrew. That result is worth holding on to while reading what designers do to their own rooms.

2Anna, in Rotterdam, had the original open floor divided into four the year she took over, and has since had two more walls put in. She also had a ping-pong table placed in the middle of the largest room. Twenty minutes of mindless play, she says, sparks more than an afternoon of meetings ever has. The desks were specially built to be raised by hand, because she wanted people to stand up without asking anybody first, and she had the booking system rewritten twice until it was user-friendly enough that nobody came to her about it.

3Tomas works above a shop in Ljubljana. He got the lamp posts outside the door yarn-bombed by a local knitting group, which cost him a week of arguments with the city and one afternoon of wool. The lights in the yard run on wind power from a turbine he had attached to the roof by an electrician. None of this is decoration, he insists: everything had to be practical first, and the wool is there because the street was grey and nobody was going to have it repainted for him.

4Kiro, in Lagos, has had a slide built from the studio down to the lobby, and admits that it is a perk rather than a working condition — original, photogenic, and used about twice a week. What he defends is the room next to it, where a twenty-minute nap is treated as work rather than as time off. He gets his whole team sent outside at four to recharge, and a swing on the balcony is used by whoever gets there first. Friday afternoons off are a treat, he says. The nap room is not.

5Read together, the three have something in common that none of them mentions. Not one of them had the space designed for them in advance. Every change was made after watching the room fail at something: Anna put the walls back because nobody was concentrating, Tomas had the turbine fitted because the yard was unusable after dark, Kiro built the nap room because his team were sleeping badly and lying about it. The slide was the exception, and it is the one he defends least.

6That pattern fits the research better than the brochures do. An open plan is designed for an imagined worker who becomes more sociable when observed; the evidence says the opposite happens. What these three had done, in their different ways, was put boundaries back — a wall, a door, a room with one clear purpose — and then defend them. It is a less impressive photograph than a slide. It is probably why the rooms work.

Text A · Three rooms, three sets of changes

Anna, in Rotterdam, had the original open floor divided into four the year she took over, and has since had two more walls put in. She also had a ping-pong table placed in the middle of the largest room. Twenty minutes of mindless play, she says, sparks more than an afternoon of meetings ever has. The desks were specially built to be raised by hand, because she wanted people to stand up without asking anybody first, and she had the booking system rewritten twice until it was user-friendly enough that nobody came to her about it.

Tomas works above a shop in Ljubljana. He got the lamp posts outside the door yarn-bombed by a local knitting group, which cost him a week of arguments with the city and one afternoon of wool. The lights in the yard run on wind power from a turbine he had attached to the roof by an electrician. None of this is decoration, he insists: everything had to be practical first, and the wool is there because the street was grey and nobody was going to have it repainted for him.

Kiro, in Lagos, has had a slide built from the studio down to the lobby, and admits that it is a perk rather than a working condition — original, photogenic, and used about twice a week. What he defends is the room next to it, where a twenty-minute nap is treated as work rather than as time off. He gets his whole team sent outside at four to recharge, and a swing on the balcony is used by whoever gets there first. Friday afternoons off are a treat, he says. The nap room is not.

Text B · Why the pattern is the opposite of the brochure

Written for this course, from Bernstein & Turban, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 373:20170239 (2018).

The standard argument for the open office is that removing walls makes people talk to each other. In 2018 two researchers tested it properly, tracking employees at two corporate headquarters with wearable sensors and message logs before and after the walls came down. Face-to-face interaction fell by roughly seventy per cent in both cases, and email and instant messaging rose to replace it. People who could be seen at all times withdrew.

Read against that finding, the three rooms have something in common that none of their owners mentions. Not one of them had the space designed for them in advance. Every change was made after watching the room fail at something: Anna had the walls put back because nobody was concentrating, Tomas had the turbine fitted because the yard was unusable after dark, Kiro had the nap room built because his team were sleeping badly and lying about it. None of them got a consultant in first; each of them had the answer built after the problem had appeared. The slide was the exception, and it is the one he defends least.

That pattern fits the research better than the brochures do. An open plan is designed for an imagined worker who becomes more sociable when observed; the evidence says the opposite happens. A company that has its walls taken out to encourage conversation usually gets the conversation moved onto a screen instead. What these three had done, in their different ways, was put boundaries back — a wall, a door, a room with one clear purpose — and then defend them against the argument that a workplace should look open. It is a less impressive photograph than a slide, and it is harder to have copied, because what has to be copied is the noticing rather than the object. It is probably why the rooms work.

1 · Read the explanation.
Have something done, and its relatives

The pattern. have (or get) + the thing + past participle: She had the walls put in. The order never changes, and the participle never moves in front of the object. It says that the subject arranged the work and somebody else carried it out. Who that somebody was is usually left out, because it is not the point; add it with by only when it is: He got the posts yarn-bombed by a knitting group.

Have or get. They mean the same thing. Get is more informal, commoner in speech, and often carries a hint that it took some organising: I finally got the roof fixed. In writing, have is safer.

All tenses, and questions. Only the first word changes: I have my hair cut every month, I had it cut yesterday, I am having it cut on Friday, I have had it cut twice this year, I will have it cut before the interview, I want to have it cut. Questions and negatives use do: Did you have it cut? / I did not have it cut.

When the person is named. Two other patterns exist. have somebody do something (no to) is close to giving an instruction: She had a builder put the walls in. get somebody to do something (with to) suggests persuading: She got a builder to put the walls in. Both name the worker; have something done does not.

The unwelcome use. The same words describe something bad that happened to you, with nobody arranging anything: He had his bike stolen, She had her flight cancelled. Only the context tells the two apart, and context always does.

The commonest errors at this level
  • Wrong order: She had put in the walls means she did it herself.
  • Infinitive instead of participle: I had my hair to cut, I got the roof to fix.
  • To after have + person: She had a builder to put them in.
  • No to after get + person: She got a builder put them in.
  • Forgetting do in questions: Had you your hair cut?

Two things to watch

1 — The order carries the meaning. She had the walls put in and She had put in the walls are different sentences: the first is a client, the second is a past perfect and a person with a hammer. The object must sit between the two verbs.

2 — Two get patterns, one small word. Get something done takes a participle; get somebody to do something takes to and the infinitive. Mixing them is the single commonest mistake in this area.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Turning a plain sentence into have something done

Start: A developer rewrote the booking system for Anna last year. We want to tell it from Anna’s side.

Step 1 — find the thing that was worked on. Not the developer, not Anna: the booking system. That noun goes in the middle.

Step 2 — choose the tense on have. The work is finished and dated, so past simple: had.

Step 3 — put the verb into the participle. Rewrite → wrote → rewritten. Never the middle form.

Step 4 — decide about the worker. Drop a developer, or keep it with by if it is the point. Here it is not.

Result: Anna had the booking system rewritten last year.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Three words, one fixed order

have + the thing + past participle: She had the walls put in. The subject arranged the work; somebody else did it. The order is not negotiable — She had put in the walls is a different sentence (past perfect, and she did it herself).

The tense lives in have, exactly as it lives in be in the passive: I have my hair cut every month · We are having the office repainted · He had a turbine attached to the roof · She has had two walls put in · They will have the slide built in March · You should have that lock changed · He wants to have the system rewritten.

get, the person version, and the unwelcome version

get + object + participle is the informal equivalent, and often carries the sense of effort or persuasion: He got the posts yarn-bombed. Name the agent only when it is news: He got them yarn-bombed by a knitting group.

When you want to name the person who does the work, the structure changes: have + person + bare infinitive — the person was told: She had a builder put the walls in. get + person + to + infinitive — the person was persuaded: She got a builder to put the walls in. Note the to after get and the absence of it after have; this is the detail that separates a B2 answer from a B1 one.

Finally, the same shape reports something unwelcome that nobody arranged: He had his bike stolen · She had her flight cancelled. Context tells you which reading is meant — nobody arranges a theft.

Errors to watch: She had put the walls in (meaning she arranged it) → had the walls put in · She had a builder to put them in → no to after have · She got a builder put them in → to put · I am having cut my hair → having my hair cut.

A proposal for the room you work in

The brief

1 · Read the model proposal.
Model · a proposal for three changes

Our office is one long room with eleven desks, two windows at the far end and a printer nobody can hear over. The complaint I hear most often is not about space: it is that there is nowhere to take a phone call, so calls are taken in the corridor, standing up.

First, I would have the storage corner turned into a small room with a door. A carpenter could do it in three days, and the shelves are already there. It would not be original, and nobody would photograph it, but it is the change people have been asking for since the original open plan was decided on above our heads.

Second, I would get the printer moved to the corridor and have the two nearest desks placed where it stood. That costs nothing, and the noise problem is solved in an afternoon by somebody with a trolley.

Third, I would have the booking system for the meeting room rewritten so that it is user-friendly enough to use from a phone. At the moment people simply walk in, which is practical for them and useless for everybody else.

If only one can be funded, it should be the first. A slide would be a treat; a door is a working condition.
